item.title: Man Who Told of a Childhood With Wolves Dies at 80
item.description:
Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja, whose account of growing up in a remote part of Spain, with the companionship of only wolves and other animals, was analyzed in a case study and adapted into literature and film, died this month at 80, according to the authorities in San Cibrao das Viñas, the municipality where he spent his final years.

Mr. Rodríguez’s story came to light in the mid-1970s, about a decade after he had made what he described as an unwilling return to human society. Gabriel Janer Manila, a writer, heard about the case from a friend and wanted to learn more.

“At first, it seemed like a fabrication. It couldn’t be true,” Mr. Janer said in a 2010 interview with the site Anika Entre Libros.

But he came to believe to believe the tale, finding corroboration for Mr. Rodríguez’s claims from witnesses and other research. Mr. Janer would go on to write a study about Mr. Rodríguez’s childhood and, later, a novel called “I Played With Wolves,” originally published in 2009.

The story also inspired a 2010 film directed by Gerardo Oliveras, “Among Wolves,” in which Mr. Rodríguez appeared.

Mr. Rodríguez faced doubts over the years, but his story fascinated many. Mr. Janer became convinced after visiting places Mr. Rodríguez said he had been and meeting people — including a seminarian who had cared for him — who backed up the story and spoke of Mr. Rodríguez’s complete lack of social know-how.

In Rante, a village in San Cibrao das Viñas, in northwest Spain, where Mr. Rodríguez lived for the last quarter-century of his life, some people told Germany’s public broadcaster around the time the film was released that they had doubted his story until it was made into a movie — and some said they continued to be dubious. In 2010, a team from Spain’s public broadcaster traveled with Mr. Rodríguez to the place where he said he had lived, filming him showing some of his survival skills, like catching fish using rocks, and his deep familiarity with nature, including mimicking bird calls.

In any case, he eventually came to be known as the “wolf boy of Sierra Morena” and stuck to the story over the decades.

Claims of having grown up in the wild are widely viewed with skepticism, and expertise in the subject is rare. There have been some notable cases, though they are few. Feral children also appeared in ancient myths and medieval folk tales, fueling a real-life fascination with them.

In 1726, Caroline, the Princess of Wales, sought the guardianship of a youth found in the woods in Germany who became known as Peter the Wild Boy and was a source of wonder in Europe. She installed him in her house in London under the watch of a doctor, then put him in the care of a servant when he proved unruly. The so-called Wild Boy of Aveyron was found in France at the end of the 18th century and was taken to a physician in Paris who tried and failed to teach him society’s ways.

Such tales have intrigued people because they say as much about society as they do about the children said to have lived outside of it. “Through the stories, factual and fictional, of the feral children, there emerges, perhaps, another narrative: the fragmented and haunting story of our continuing relationship with the savage image of ourselves,” the cultural historian Michael Newton wrote in his 2002 book, “Savage Girls and Wild Boys: A History of Feral Children.”

As Mr. Rodríguez told it, he was born into a poor family in southern Spain in June 1946. His mother died when he was very young, and the woman his father later married was an abusive stepmother. The family lived in a remote alpine hut in the Sierra Morena mountain range, turning firewood into charcoal. When he was about 7, he said, he was put in the care of an old goatherd, to be trained to replace him.

“He takes Marcos in and teaches him how to survive, how to care for the flock of goats, how to do everything that might help him,” Mr. Janer said in the 2010 interview.

The old man then died or disappeared, and young Marcos began to fend for himself, unwilling or unable to return to his former home.

Mr. Rodríguez said he lived in the wild for about 11 years with the help of wolves and other animals. In 1965, he was discovered by law enforcement authorities among wolves, wearing animal skins.

He described his return to life among humans as something he did not know how to manage and would never fully embrace. According to Mr. Rodríguez’s interviews and Mr. Janer’s study, his rehabilitation was undertaken by nuns. He said he had lost the habits of walking upright and of using human speech, and he had forgotten how to behave with people.

Mr. Rodríguez said he struggled with human society for much of his life. Employers had taken advantage of him over the years, people had mocked him and he had been happiest among the animals, he said in interviews.

In Rante, he worked with Amigas das Árbores, an environmental group, speaking to children at schools about his youth and his unique experience with animals.

The group, in a post on social media earlier this month, said that one of his final wishes had been “for his ashes to remain in the village that took him in.”

In an interview with the newspaper El País in 2018, Mr. Rodríguez said that despite his disappointment with humanity, he had no chance of returning to a life in the mountains. The area where he had once lived now featured cottages connected to the electric grid, and the wolves were strangers.

“If I call out to them they are going to respond, but they are not going to approach me,” he said. “I smell like people.”

item.title: Syria and Israel Hold U.S.-Mediated Talks to Try to Ease Tensions
item.description:
Syria and Israel held talks in Jordan on Sunday to ease tensions between the two countries, according to Syria’s state news agency, days after Israel struck an air base in Syrian territory.

The talks, mediated by the United States, focused on creating mechanisms to stop Israeli operations on Syrian territory and on reviving talks about a security agreement between Syria and Israel, according to the news agency, SANA, citing an official at the Syrian Foreign Ministry.

The Syrian delegation was led by Asaad al-Shaibani, the foreign minister, and included the heads of Syria’s general intelligence and military intelligence agencies, SANA noted.

Israeli officials have not publicly commented on the talks and did not immediately respond to requests for further information.

The two sides also discussed efforts to prevent tensions between Turkey and Israel — both of which neighbor Syria — from spilling over into Syrian territory, SANA reported. The Israeli strikes on the Syrian air base last week followed a visit by a Turkish delegation to the airfield as part of discussions to rehabilitate the site, according to Syrian and Israeli officials.

The talks on Sunday were the latest sign that President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria was open to diplomacy with Israel, a stark departure from his predecessors, who maintained a decades-long hostility toward the country. Mr. al-Sharaa’s government first engaged with Israel in U.S.-brokered back-channel discussions last year — the first such talks in more than a decade.

That diplomatic track stalled after the American-Israeli war on Iran erupted this year.

So far, the discussions over the past year have not curbed Israel’s military activity in Syria since rebels led by Mr. al-Sharaa swept into the capital, Damascus, in 2024 and overthrew the Assad government.

The Israeli military has launched hundreds of airstrikes on military targets in Syria; deployed forces deep into parts of the country’s south, near its border with Israel; and built military outposts and supporting infrastructure in Syrian territory near the Israeli border, according to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a nonprofit that tracks global conflict.

Israeli officials have defended the actions as necessary to ensure that hostile forces such as Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group; or the Islamic State, which remains active in Syria, cannot entrench themselves near Israel.

But in Syria, the military interventions have stoked fears that Israel is seeking to maintain a long-term military presence on Syrian territory and may expand operations beyond the southern border areas.

The Trump administration — a proponent of Syria’s new government — has pushed for discussions between the two countries and publicly called for Syria to join the Abraham Accords, which established diplomatic relations between Israel and four Arab states during Mr. Trump’s first term. Syrian officials have shown no inclination to do so imminently, and the scope of the latest round of talks were more limited.

After Israel struck the air base in northwestern Syria last week, the government in Damascus said that the strikes were “an unjustified act of aggression, a flagrant violation of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region.”

item.title: Iran Pledges to Defy Trump’s Escalating Sanctions
item.description:
Iranian officials brushed off the U.S. announcement on Monday of more economic sanctions against their country and the threat of even stronger actions to come.

Seyed Ali Madanizadeh, the finance minister, said that Iran was already prepared to deal with American efforts to further isolate it from the world economy.

“The government has a two-year plan for the country’s economic affairs, and all matters have been covered in this plan,” he said in an interview on state media after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the additional economic pressure. “Sanctions are not new” to Iran, Mr. Madanizadeh added.

Iran’s influential Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said that Washington’s new economic campaign would only punish the Iranian people.

“By waging economic warfare and imposing multilayered sanctions, the enemy seeks to sow despair, put pressure on people’s livelihoods and undermine social trust,” the Guards Corp said in a statement on Iranian state media shortly after Mr. Bessent’s announcement.

Mr. Bessent said that more than “60 entities, individuals, and vessels across the world that enable the Iranian regime to procure illicit nuclear and missile technology, conduct cyber operations, and generate oil revenue” had been sanctioned and that the United States would soon take additional steps to “collapse every last option for Iran.”

The new sanctions target Mr. Bessent said were “five of Iran‘s most vital lifelines that it exploits in other countries: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.” The campaign “will gather force with every day that follows,” he said.

President Trump had pledged that the war he began alongside Israel in late February would be swift and decisive, but the conflict has dragged on with no clear end in sight. A cease-fire signed in June collapsed weeks later after Iran resumed its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical Persian Gulf waterway for oil and gas.

Now, Mr. Trump has threatened Iran with “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale.” He has also warned that countries doing business with Iran would face severe penalties. Iran’s largest trading partners include China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.

The U.A.E. last week said it was halting all trade and financial transactions with Iran. It is unclear if the United States played a role in the Emirates’ decision, but the announcement came hours after a call from President Trump to the Emirati leader, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed.

Analysts say Iran is more likely to lash out militarily in response to heightened American economic pressure than to accept Mr. Trump’s demands that it curb its nuclear program and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Many experts are also skeptical that Mr. Trump will impose serious penalties on China, whose leader, Xi Jinping, is slated to visit Washington next month. Mr. Bessent said that no one was exempt from the economic pressure campaign on Iran but declined to respond to questions about China specifically.

“The United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of the Iranian Parliament, wrote on social media minutes before Mr. Bessent spoke. Mr. Ghalibaf dismissed the U.S. effort as “bombast.”

Western sanctions have squeezed Iran for years, fueling inflation, unemployment and other economic ills that helped to stoke mass protests against the Iranian government earlier this year. But Iran’s leaders have not bent, and they responded to the unrest with a brutal and bloody crackdown that killed thousands of demonstrators, according to Iranian rights groups operating in exile.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry similarly said on Monday that Tehran would not bow to the escalating pressure. Esmaeil Baghaei, the ministry spokesman, speaking before Mr. Bessent’s announcement, said the Trump administration was merely “repeating methods that have proven unsuccessful.”

“Iran will certainly use all multilateral capacities to counter economic sanctions,” he told reporters at a news conference.

On Sunday night, Mohsen Rezaei, a senior Iranian official, threatened that Iran could respond to economic pressure by retaliating against American allies in the Persian Gulf. If the U.S.-led campaign continued, “not a single drop of oil will be exported” from the region, he wrote on social media.

“Iran will regard any country’s participation in or support for America’s economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war,” said Mr. Rezaei, who leads Iran’s powerful Supreme National Security Council.

Gulf Arab countries have already borne the brunt of Iranian retaliation for the U.S.-Israeli campaign. Iran has fired drones and missiles at American bases in those countries, and it has effectively blockaded oil and gas exports via the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: British Leader Arrives in Ukraine as Russia Amps Up Warnings
item.description:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain arrived in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, on Monday, taking a brief break from his focus on economic issues at home to make his first foreign trip since taking office.

Mr. Burnham’s visit comes as Russia has sharpened verbal attacks against Britain’s longstanding assistance to Ukraine, warning of consequences if the aid and support continue.

Mr. Burnham appeared to shrug off those warnings on Monday as British officials announced that he would present President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine with technical plans for a long-range missile.

The missile, jointly built with France, is known as the Storm Shadow in Britain. Officials said that allowing the classified plans to be provided to Kyiv would allow Ukraine and France to build the French version, known as SCALP, on assembly lines inside Ukraine.

Mr. Burnham arrived in Kyiv by train on Monday morning after traveling overnight.

In a statement released by his office, Mr. Burnham said: “The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.”

He added: “Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”

Mr. Burnham is expected to meet with Mr. Zelensky and will be chairman of a meeting of the “coalition of the willing,” a group of leaders who have pledged support for Ukraine in the war against Russia.

Katarina Mathernova, the European Union’s ambassador to Ukraine, told reporters on Sunday night as she traveled for the coalition meeting that the mood in Ukraine had “darkened” this summer amid targeted Russian attacks on civilians.

She also noted that the war seemed to be moving into a new phase in which both sides try to inflict serious economic damage on the other. Russia is choking off Ukraine’s grain exports through the Black Sea, and Ukraine is targeting economic actors, like Wildberries, a company that is Russia’s equivalent to Amazon.

Jeanna Smialek contributed reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine.

item.title: Gripped by El Niño, Indonesia Battles Intensifying Wildfires
item.description:
The wildfires have been burning in the peatlands for weeks, belching acrid smoke over West Kalimantan Province in Indonesian Borneo. In the capital, Pontianak, everyone in Alfian Effendi’s family has developed coughs.

The thick haze, which has also drifted into Malaysia, has forced schools in the area to temporarily suspend classes, including for Mr. Alfian’s four children, whose noses are running from the smoke. Local officials have distributed masks and urged people to stay indoors. But that is a luxury that Mr. Alfian, 37, the owner of a chicken slaughterhouse, said he does not have.

“We all have to work to earn a living, right?” he said in a phone interview. “We know we are risking our health, but what choice do we have?”

Wildfires are a seasonal occurrence in many parts of Indonesia, a vast archipelagic country, so this trade-off is nothing new for Mr. Alfian. But there is reason to fear that this year may be especially bad, according to experts. Indonesia is in the grip of a “super” El Niño that will likely suppress the rains that would otherwise extinguish the fires.

And the fire season has yet to peak.

“The question now is whether the current acceleration continues through September and October and first two weeks of November,” said David Gaveau, a landscape ecologist and the founder of Nusantara Atlas, a website that tracks fires and deforestation in the region. “New mega fires may appear in southern Sumatra in September,” he added, referring to Indonesia’s third-largest island.

As of Aug. 20, there were more than 224,000 hot spots suggesting fire activity across Indonesia, according to Nusantara Atlas’s satellite data. Mr. Gaveau said that this was an unusually high number that resembled the trend in 2019, one of Indonesia’s worst fire seasons, in which he said as much as 7.7 million acres of land burned.

There are other worrying signs. About 230,000 acres of land burned in July alone, roughly equal to the total area affected between January and June, based on data from Indonesia’s forest ministry.

Many of Indonesia’s most devastating fire seasons have developed during strong El Niño events, in which the warming of the central Pacific Ocean shifts rain patterns, drenching some areas while drying out others.

In 2015, another El Niño year, the government said about 6.4 million acres burned, sending smoke beyond Indonesia’s borders. A study by researchers from Harvard and Columbia universities later estimated that the haze from the fires contributed to around 100,000 premature deaths across Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

Climate experts have noted that this year’s El Niño may end up being particularly formidable — the strongest in recorded history, according to some estimates.

Mr. Alfian said that he can already sense its effects in Pontianak, where he said the earth has been so hot and dry that it feels like even an errant spark could explode into flames, and the local river has become so depleted that seawater is rushing in, making the tap water salty.

“We can only use it for baths now,” he said. “For cooking or washing our vegetables, we have to buy extra gallons of water.”

Though El Niño has historically been a major accelerant for fires, experts point to the widespread degradation of Indonesia’s peatlands as the underlying reason for the country’s growing fire risk over the past few decades.

In their natural state, peatlands, a type of spongy wetland that makes up around 10 percent of the country’s total land mass, are resistant to fire because they are composed of waterlogged decaying organic matter. But decades of industrialized agriculture, such as those used for palm oil, one of Indonesia’s biggest exports, have led to the mass draining of them.

“The exposed, dry peat becomes combustible fuel,” said Resti Salmayenti, a tropical peatland researcher at the University of Leeds. “And once ignited, fires can spread below the surface, where they’re hard to detect and can burn for a long time during prolonged drought, like during El Niño.”

In addition to harming respiratory health, those fires also produce disproportionately large greenhouse emissions because peatland stores far more carbon than forests.

Though Indonesian law requires companies operating within significant peatlands to keep them wet, Bambang Saharjo, a forest fire forensics expert at IPB University in Bogor, West Java, said that those rules are often ignored, while broader peatland restoration efforts, like using canal blocks to trap water, have also stalled.

“Many canal blocks and boreholes have fallen into disrepair, rendering them ineffective for fire suppression and leading to an escalation of increasingly massive fires,” he said.

In nearly all cases, he added, human activity is responsible for causing this damaged peatland to catch fire, such as companies or people burning them to free up usable land. Indonesian authorities have so far arrested more than 70 people and launched investigations into at least four companies in connection with the ongoing fires.

Officials have also turned to cloud-seeding, a weather modification technique that involves using planes to spray particles like silver iodide and salt in the air to trigger rainfall. But the method is only effective if there is already moisture in the clouds, so experts say the benefits may be limited.

The same scarcity is being felt on the ground in West Kalimantan, where Bimpi Permata Restu, a volunteer firefighter, has been racing across the parched landscape on a motorbike outfitted with a pump and hose, dousing vegetation to keep it from catching fire.

“The challenge for now is the dried-up water sources,” he said.

Mr. Bimpi, 25, first started volunteering to fight fires as a teenager. Now he has a two-year-old child with another on the way. Their home is encircled by hot spots that spew smoke and fill him with anxiety about his family’s health.

item.title: Can ‘Argentina’s Texas’ Save the Country’s Economy?
item.description:
Much of the sun-bleached desert in northwest Patagonia looks like it did 100 million years ago: a vast, prehistoric expanse where the world’s biggest dinosaurs once roamed.

But a different kind of behemoth has now come roaring in, with towering rigs advancing across the desert floor and burrowing deep beneath it in a furious rush for oil and gas.

The rigs’ gigantic iron legs are extracting shale oil and gas at levels never seen in Argentina before, turning a quiet stretch of the country into the thrumming center of a new oil and gas boom that is fueling a wave of optimism about the future.

“We reached the promised land,” said Raúl Krasuk, 69, who manages wells at the site for Vista, an Argentine energy company, as he sat in an oil field cafeteria that serves chicken breasts to workers who have come from all over Argentina for a slice of the bonanza.

President Javier Milei has called the oil and gas deposit — known as Vaca Muerta, or Dead Cow — a “panacea” for Argentina, with the potential to solve the country’s chronic economic instability by flooding it with dollars from exports. He has bet heavily on the project.

For the first time in the country’s history, crude oil overtook soy flour as the top export this year. Now, many in the oil sector invoke the promise of a second boom after the agricultural surge that, over a century ago, turned Argentina into one of the world’s richest countries.

“This is the big opportunity Argentina has to prosper,” said Rolando Figueroa, the governor of the Neuquén province, home to the shale-rich area many refer to as Argentina’s Texas.

The hedge fund of the American billionaire Peter Thiel, who has established a foothold in Argentina, recently reported that it had acquired over $76 million worth of Vista shares.

Still, many question whether Vaca Muerta can truly catalyze the economic rebirth of Argentina, a country hobbled in recent decades by soaring inflation and currency crises. Many businesses are closing as Mr. Milei’s austerity measures have weakened domestic demand, while lower trade barriers have opened local firms to cheaper competition, stoking skepticism that the oil boom can generate enough jobs to absorb widespread losses elsewhere.

The economic sectors thriving under Mr. Milei — energy and mining — create relatively few jobs, while labor-intensive ones like manufacturing or retail are suffering.

Mr. Milei says that Vaca Muerta will drive broader economic activity, but for now, many workers partaking in the black gold rush arrived on buses with nothing but a backpack and a tent as they fled low pay or a lack of work elsewhere.

So many hopefuls flooded into Añelo, the town closest to the oil and gas reserves, that the mayor has pleaded with outsiders to stop coming.

“There isn’t so much work for everyone,” the mayor, Fernando Banderet, said on Argentine radio last month.

The booming energy sector brings a fresh and much-needed inflow of dollars to cash-starved Argentina, securing it a larger role in global energy markets squeezed by the conflict in Iran. Still, the reliance on fracking is raising local environmental alarms and questions over committing the nation’s future to fossil fuels that much of the world only recently pledged to leave behind.

Despite these questions, and challenges, what is clear is that much of the country has its eyes on Vaca Muerta.

“It’s a revolution,” said Mr. Banderet.

Mr. Banderet arrived in Añelo as a child when it was a small, deprived rural community. He spent much of his youth living in a converted bus, became a father at 16, and started work as a fruit picker.

Now everything has changed. As foreign governments and entrepreneurs courted him for oil-related opportunities in Añelo, he said he attended President Trump’s second inauguration, went on a trip to Israel, and traveled to the Cannes film festival.

“It is the Vaca Muerta fever,” he said.

In the past two years, thousands of people have arrived in Añelo. Some initially slept in tents until they could afford a bed in one of the prefabricated housing units that have popped up almost overnight. Añelo’s population doubled in the past two years,to 12,000, Mr. Banderet said, the sound of hammers pounding behind him as the town hall was expanded.

Thrumming had become the town’s soundtrack — a chorus of engines from the oil workers’ white pickups that jam the main road, the grind of cement mixers churning fresh concrete, and the roar of drilling rigs in the distance.

On a recent evening, Sabino Poblete, 46, was at work building new apartments, the desert dusk bathing the bare concrete pillars in orange, as the flames from gas flares flickered on the horizon. Mr. Poblete had arrived in Añelo just five days before from Argentina’s central city of Cordoba, hitchhiking with a backpack and a tent. “I came to try my luck,” he said.

At the nearby gas station, other migrant workers waited for a bus.

“Everywhere they say this is the oil capital,” said Ezequiel Barrozo, 27, who migrated to Añelo from the city of Rosario this year. He tripled his policeman’s salary back home, he said, by finding construction work in Añelo. “People told me that if I came here I would have a great opportunity,” he said.

This wild west optimism is visible throughout the province of Neuquén, which surrounds Añelo. Restaurants are full, and hotels and residential complexes are rising, with names like the Shale Hotel or Petroleum Housing Complex. Shopping malls and truck dealerships are sprouting across barren expanses long ruled by winds and dinosaur bones.

High above the banks of the Limay River, young engineers from across Argentina sit in Vista’s high-tech control room remotely monitoring extraction sites.

A few miles away, young Argentines learn oil-field trades free of charge, in a new training institute sponsored by Argentina’s state-controlled oil company, YPF, and other industry players. On a recent afternoon, students used gamelike control stations for immersive work simulations. In a country where huge numbers of young professionals seek opportunities abroad, these students said that they were excited about their careers at home.

“Hello, future of the country!” the school’s director, Gustavo Livoreiro, said as he entered a classroom.

A new vision of the country was emerging in Neuquén — an image different from the fertile farmlands and their gauchos, which have long defined the nation. Here Argentina’s future looks like massive petrol tanks with metallic trunks pointed toward the desert sky, and it smells of diesel as men covered in mud haul drill pipes out from deep inside the Earth.

The Vaca Muerta shale formation, which holds the world’s fourth-largest reserves for shale oil and second-largest for shale gas, had been known for decades, but Argentina only recently secured the investment and imported the advanced technology necessary to extract them at a large scale. Now Argentina produces over 850,000 oil barrels a day, up from about 500,000 a decade ago.

Over the past 10 years, Vaca Muerta has helped transform Argentina’s multi-billion-dollar energy deficit into a surplus, with greater gains expected in the future — especially amid global crises that heightened the appeal of a stable, conflict-free energy supply.

Mr. Milei has championed the energy sector with major investment tax breaks and made it easier to export fuel, driving progress on a vital new pipeline. Though past Argentine governments laid the groundwork in Vaca Muerta, Mr. Milei’s administration now stands to harvest its rewards.

The shale exploitation, combined with a new budget tightening by the government, marks “a structural, fundamental, transformational change,” said Marcelo Mindlin, the chairman of Pampa Energía, one of Argentina’s largest energy companies.

“Argentina has been a symbol of instability,” he said. “These two shifts have a real chance to rewrite that history.”

This confidence is not universal. Argentina remains sharply divided about the country’s new direction.

Critics point out that while machinery is roaring in the oil patch, in industrial hubs like the Buenos Aires province, assembly lines have fallen quiet.

The disparity is visible in Neuquén. Many of those who work outside the energy ecosystem — like teachers or municipal workers — are being priced out of basic living. Even here in the country’s energy capital, Mr. Milei’s removal of state subsidies has made gas more expensive for many. Some, including some Mapuche Indigenous communities, lack gas connections to their homes.

“This is the paradox of the new Argentina,” said Lef Nawel, a Mapuche activist in Neuquén. “Either you are in or you are out.”

The Mapuche, who hold some of the deepest ties to the land where these operations take place, have been the most staunch opponents of fracking.

They protest polluting gas flares, say chemical waste from the plants is often improperly handled, and warn that the industry’s water consumption threatens to deplete rivers already suffering the effects of climate change.

“They extract the oil and take it away,” said Olga Mabel Campo, a Mapuche community leader. “But we are the ones who stay.”

Ms. Campo’s son is an oil worker. Despite her opposition, it was the best work he could find in town, she said.

When an iron wrench spun out of control and struck his face, it knocked out all his teeth and lacerated his mouth. On another occasion, a fall from a rig platform fractured his spine and broke his leg.

Thanks to the workers’ compensation payout, she said, he was able to build a house in Añelo. And he keeps working in the industry.

“It’s something impossible to stop,” Ms. Campo said. “They say Vaca Muerta is going to save the world.”
